quote: 20.1 Vendor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Customer, its Affiliates, and their directors, officers, employees, and agents from each third-party claim and resulting damages, settlements, judgments, penalties, costs, and reasonable attorneys' fees arising from an allegation that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate an intellectual property right.
rationale: Section 20 meets the preferred position in full. 20.1 gives an express Vendor duty to defend, indemnify and hold harmless Customer, its Affiliates and their personnel against third-party claims that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate IP. 20.2 extends the same defence and indemnity to Vendor's breach of Applicable Law, unauthorized access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor, and Vendor's gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud. 20.4 supplies the standard procedure — prompt notice, reasonable cooperation (at the indemnifying Party's expense) and control of the defence — with a settlement-consent protection favouring the indemnified party. Customer's reciprocal indemnity in 20.3 is properly narrow: only unmodified Customer-supplied material used strictly as authorized, plus Customer's own violation of Applicable Law, with carve-backs for Vendor Technology, modification, combination or instructions. Beyond the preferred checklist, 20.5 adds the procure/modify/replace/refund remedy ladder (cross-referenced by the 9.3 termination right), and 21.3 treats indemnification obligations as Excluded Claims, so Vendor's indemnity is uncapped rather than subject to the fallback 3× super-cap. No redline is warranted.

rationale: The IP package meets the preferred position in full, so no redline is warranted. § 14.2 vests ownership of each Deliverable created specifically for Customer in Customer on creation and contains an express present assignment of all worldwide right, title and interest (plus personnel assignments and further-assurance). § 14.3, read with the § 1.8 definition, confirms Vendor retains only its pre-existing Vendor Technology, and § 13.2 grants Customer and its Affiliates a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid licence to use, modify and create derivative works from Vendor Technology embedded in a Deliverable. § 14.1 confirms Customer owns all Customer Data and that Vendor receives only a limited right to process it solely to provide, secure, support and improve the Services for Customer — service delivery, not independent exploitation — reinforced by § 15.1's bar on sale, advertising, cross-customer combination and model training. § 14.4 negates joint ownership absent a separately signed instrument, and limits feedback use to generalized suggestions while Customer retains unrestricted rights in its own feedback. Two points are noted only for the record and are not deviations: Deliverable ownership is "subject to payment of the applicable Fees" (customary), and the § 1.3 carve-out of anonymized operational telemetry that cannot reasonably be linked to Customer, an Authorized User or an individual is an acceptable de-identified-telemetry exclusion.

quote: 21.1 Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of the Fees paid or payable by Customer during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: Section 21 meets our preferred position on its material terms, so it sits above the fallback and we do not redline it. § 21.1 imposes an expressly mutual aggregate cap at the greater of Fees paid or payable in the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000; § 21.2 excludes indirect, incidental, special, exemplary, punitive and consequential damages mutually (and helpfully confirms data-restoration, replacement-service, notice and incident-response costs are direct damages); § 21.3 places confidentiality, data-protection and security breaches, indemnification obligations, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and infringement of the other Party's IP outside the cap as Excluded Claims. "Fees" (§ 1.5) is a substantive revenue measure (recurring subscription, professional services and usage fees), so the cap basis is not illusory. Two minor points noted but not flagged: the payment carve-out in § 21.3 is limited to "undisputed Fees for conforming Services" rather than all amounts due — a narrowing that runs in our favour — and taxes/expenses/implementation charges are excluded from the Fees measure, which is a standard drafting nuance rather than a fallback failure. No hidden one-sided cap exists: § 20 leaves indemnities uncapped and § 18.2 states insurance does not limit Vendor's liabilities.

No convenience termination right exists for Customer anywhere (27.3 is force-majeure specific; 6.2, 19.4 and 20.5 are remedy-based), which is a deviation in a term longer than 12 months. Retained 10.2 refunds only "prepaid recurring Fees covering the period after termination", which is narrower than prepaid Fees as defined in 1.5 and is not an express pro-rata refund, so it does not satisfy the refund element. We therefore insert a single new 9.4 carrying all four preferred elements: a Customer convenience right over the Agreement or any Order Form, thirty days' written notice, a pro-rata refund of all prepaid Fees for the post-termination period, and an express bar on Vendor convenience termination during a committed term. Fallback is unavailable at 30 days' notice, so the cure is drafted at the preferred level.

quote: 7.2 Customer shall offer Vendor terms no less favourable than the best terms Customer offers any other technology supplier.
rationale: Section 7.2 (the first of two clauses numbered 7.2) imposes an MFN running against us: we must extend Vendor terms no less favourable than the best terms we give any other technology supplier. It is unlimited as to product, duration, and comparison methodology, so it falls in walk-away territory and fails every fallback element (defined product, 12-month cap, like-for-like carve-outs). Section 12.3's acknowledgement that Customer has made no most-favoured-customer commitment contradicts but does not cure the operative obligation, so we take the preferred position and remove the Customer-side MFN. No Vendor-granted MFN in our favour exists to preserve.

elements.element: Customer has no most-favoured-nation obligation benefiting Vendor.
elements.evidence: Original Section 7.2 ("Customer shall offer Vendor terms no less favourable than the best terms Customer offers any other technology supplier") is replaced in the rendered operative text with "7.2 Customer has no most-favoured-nation obligation benefiting Vendor." No other clause in the cited text imposes a best-terms or match obligation on Customer; Section 12.3 affirmatively records that Customer has made no most-favoured-customer commitment, so the operative language is internally consistent.

elements.element: The Customer MFN covers only a defined product.
elements.evidence: Vacuously satisfied: the condition does not apply because, after the edit, no Customer-side MFN obligation survives anywhere in the operative text (7.2 as rendered negates it; 12.3 confirms no most-favoured-customer commitment). With no MFN, there is no scope to confine to a defined product.

elements.element: The Customer MFN lasts no longer than 12 months.
elements.evidence: Vacuously satisfied: no Customer MFN obligation remains after the replacement of Section 7.2, so there is no duration to cap at 12 months.

elements.element: The Customer MFN contains reasonable like-for-like comparison carve-outs.

verification.notes: Preferred level is complete: the operative burden on Customer to extend Vendor the best terms given to any other technology supplier is removed and replaced by an express statement that Customer owes Vendor no MFN obligation. Fallback elements are vacuously met because the eliminated obligation leaves no Customer MFN to scope, time-limit, or qualify; the stronger preferred outcome subsumes them. Minimality holds: the edit is confined to the offending sentence in Section 7.2. No survival tails, procedures, damages categories, or unrelated boilerplate were added, and the favourable Section 12.3 acknowledgement is retained verbatim rather than duplicated or amended. Intent is preserved: no Vendor-granted MFN in Customer's favour existed to protect, no defined term is left dangling, and the new 7.2 is consistent with (rather than contradicted by) the retained Section 12.3 acknowledgement. Note only that the drafting is declaratory; if the parties prefer, striking the sentence outright would achieve the same result, but the current wording is operative and unambiguous. Drafting caution (not a defect in this checklist): the source document contained two clauses numbered 7.2; the drafter should confirm the replacement lands on the MFN clause and does not disturb the second 7.2 or any cross-references to it.

rationale: The Agreement sits at our preferred position. § 2.1 (p0012) expressly disclaims any minimum quantity or purchase commitment, confirms Customer pays only for Services ordered in an executed Order Form, and provides that declining to place further orders is neither a breach nor a shortfall. § 7.1 (p0026) reinforces this by barring any minimum-use or similar charge not identified in the Order Form, and § 12.3 (p0050) records that Customer has made no minimum-volume commitment. No take-or-pay, shortfall penalty, or volume cap on Customer usage appears anywhere in the document, so no fallback true-up or reduction mechanic is needed. The sole-and-exclusive supply undertaking in § 2.2 (p0013) is a sourcing restriction rather than a purchase or volume commitment and is addressed under the EXCLUSIVITY rule; we do not flag it twice here.

quote: 8.2 Each Order Form renews for twelve months unless either Party gives one hundred eighty days' advance written notice.
rationale: § 8.2 auto-renews each Order Form for twelve months but requires one hundred eighty days' advance notice to prevent renewal. That window exceeds both the fallback ceiling (60 days) and the 90-day walk-away threshold, so it is a material deviation. The twelve-month renewal term is acceptable, and § 8.3 already caps uplift at the lesser of CPI and three percent, satisfying the price element at both levels. We target the fallback with the single smallest change: reduce the non-renewal notice window to sixty (60) days, stated with the numeral so the threshold is unambiguous on its face. The absence of a Vendor renewal reminder and the thirty-day preferred window are noted only as short of preferred, not flagged.

verification.notes: Fallback level is complete: the single edit brings the non-renewal window to exactly 60 days, and the retained § 8.3 cap (lesser of CPI and 3%) is inside the 5% fallback ceiling. Preferred is not reached: the window is 60 rather than 30 days and there is no Vendor renewal-reminder obligation at least 60 days before renewal; these are noted as short of preferred, consistent with the rationale. Minimal: the only textual change is the numeral in § 8.2 (180 days → sixty (60) days). The 12-month renewal term, the mutual 'either Party' structure, and all of § 8.3 (CPI/3% cap, 90-day increase notice, no increase on prepaid periods) are retained verbatim; no survival tails, procedures, or extra requirements were added. Preserves intent: the renewal mechanic, Order Form references, defined terms (Order Form, Fees) and pricing/notice timing elsewhere are untouched; no dangling cross-reference, undefined trigger, or contradictory retained sentence results. Non-renewal here is natural-term expiry and is correctly evaluated under RENEWAL rather than as a convenience-termination right. Deviation classification is sound: the original 180-day window exceeded both the 60-day fallback ceiling and the 90-day walk-away threshold, so a redline was warranted rather than a rationale note.

quote: 11.1 Upon expiry or termination for any reason, Vendor shall, at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six months at the rates in the expiring Order Form.
rationale: Section 11 meets the preferred position in full: 11.1 applies "[u]pon expiry or termination for any reason" and gives up to six months' transition assistance (priced at the expiring Order Form rates, which is at least as protective as then-current rates); 11.2 requires return of all Customer Data within thirty days in a complete, commonly used, documented, machine-readable format and bars withholding for a fee dispute; and 11.3 requires secure deletion and written officer certification only after Customer confirms successful return, so certified deletion follows data return. The only nuance is that the thirty-day return clock in 11.2 runs from Customer's request rather than from termination itself, which is not a material shortfall because no deadline is imposed on when Customer may request and Section 11 expressly operates on expiry or termination. No redline needed.

The only shortfalls against preferred wording are cosmetic and not worth redlining: the malicious-code warranty is qualified to code "intentionally introduced by Vendor", and the software period is expressed as the subscription term rather than a stated twelve months.
